formulas.name: Mean
formulas.plain_english: The mean is the average of all observations—the central value around which data points cluster. In equity research, it tells you the typical return or metric over a period, forming the baseline for measuring volatility and performance.
computation: Add all values together
Divide by the count of observations

worked_example.problem: Nifty 50 monthly returns: +3%, −1%, +4%, +2%, −2%, +6%. Calculate mean return.
worked_example.insight: Over this 6-month period, Nifty 50 averaged a 2% monthly gain. This anchors variance and risk calculations.

formulas.name: Variance (Sample)
formulas.note: Bessel correction: n-1 prevents underestimating variance from sample
formulas.plain_english: Variance measures how spread out returns are from the mean. It quantifies data dispersion—higher variance means more unpredictability. In equity research, it underpins risk measurement and portfolio decisions. We divide by (n−1) for samples to avoid downward bias.
computation: Calculate deviations: subtract Mean from each Xi
Square each deviation
Sum all squared deviations
Divide by (n−1) for sample variance

worked_example.problem: From Nifty returns {+3%, −1%, +4%, +2%, −2%, +6%} with mean 2.0%, calculate sample variance.
worked_example.insight: This variance of 9.20 is relatively high, indicating Nifty returns in this period were quite volatile around the 2% mean.

formulas.name: Standard Deviation

variables.meaning: Squared deviations from mean, divided by (n−1)

formulas.plain_english: Standard deviation converts variance back into the original units (e.g., percentage returns), making it intuitive. It is the most common measure of volatility in finance—higher standard deviation means riskier, more unpredictable returns.
computation: Calculate or retrieve variance
Take its square root

worked_example.problem: From the sample variance of 9.20, calculate standard deviation.
worked_example.insight: Monthly returns deviate from the 2% mean by roughly ±3.03%, indicating moderate volatility for Nifty in this sample.

formulas.name: Correlation
formulas.plain_english: Correlation measures how two variables move together, ranging from −1 (perfect inverse) to +1 (perfect positive). In equity research, it reveals portfolio diversification potential: low or negative correlation between assets reduces portfolio risk.
computation: Calculate deviations of X from its mean and Y from its mean
Multiply paired deviations (co-movement numerator)
Sum these products
Calculate sum of squared X deviations and sum of squared Y deviations
Divide covariance by the square root of the product of the two sums

worked_example.problem: Nifty 50 monthly returns: {+3%, −1%, +4%, +2%, −2%, +6%} and Bank Nifty returns: {+2%, −2%, +5%, +1%, −3%, +7%}. Calculate correlation.
steps: Sum of Nifty squared deviations = 46; Sum of BankNifty squared deviations ≈ 80.67
worked_example.insight: Very high positive correlation (0.95) indicates Nifty and Bank Nifty move almost in lockstep. Limited diversification benefit from holding both in a portfolio.

formulas.name: Regression Slope (Beta)

variables.meaning: Market or independent variable (e.g., Nifty return)
Stock or dependent variable (e.g., TCS return)

formulas.plain_english: Regression slope (beta) tells you how much a stock moves for each 1% move in the market. A beta of 1.2 means the stock is 20% more volatile than the market; 0.8 means 20% less volatile. It is crucial for estimating systematic risk and cost of equity.
computation: Calculate deviations of X (market) and Y (stock) from their respective means
Multiply each pair of deviations
Sum the products (numerator)
Sum squared X deviations (denominator)
Divide numerator by denominator

worked_example.problem: Market (Nifty) returns: {+3%, −1%, +4%, +2%, −2%, +6%}; TCS returns: {+4%, −2%, +6%, +2%, −1%, +8%}. Calculate beta.
worked_example.insight: TCS is 26% more volatile than Nifty, meaning it amplifies market movements. Higher systematic risk demands a higher expected return.

formulas.name: Regression Intercept (Alpha)
formulas.plain_english: The intercept (alpha) is the expected return of a stock when the market return is zero. It captures the stock's excess return not explained by systematic market risk—a positive alpha suggests outperformance, though it may reflect luck or hidden risk.
computation: Calculate the mean of the dependent variable (Ybar)
Multiply beta by the mean of the independent variable (Xbar)
Subtract the product from Ybar

worked_example.problem: From the previous regression: Nifty mean = 2.0%, TCS mean = 2.83%, Beta = 1.26. Calculate alpha.
worked_example.insight: TCS has a small positive alpha of 0.31% monthly, suggesting it delivered slightly more return than its beta-based market risk would predict—though the sample is small and this may not be statistically significant.

formulas.name: R-squared
formulas.formula: Proportion of Y variance explained by X
formulas.plain_english: R-squared tells you what fraction of a stock's variance is explained by market movements. An R² of 0.70 means 70% of the stock's ups and downs come from the market; the remaining 30% is company-specific (idiosyncratic) risk. Higher R² suggests the market model is more reliable.
computation: Fit a regression line of Y on X
Calculate predicted values using the regression equation
Compute the sum of squared residuals (Y_actual − Y_predicted)²
Compute total sum of squares (Y_actual − Ybar)²
R² = 1 − (sum of squared residuals / total sum of squares), or equivalently: R² = Correlation²

worked_example.problem: From Nifty vs. TCS regression with correlation ≈ 0.95, calculate R-squared.
worked_example.insight: About 90% of TCS's monthly return variance is explained by Nifty movements, leaving only 10% to company-specific factors. This high R² indicates TCS returns are strongly tied to the broader market.

formulas.name: Annualise Monthly Std Dev
formulas.note: Volatility scales with square root of time

variables.meaning: Square root of 12 months per year

formulas.plain_english: Monthly volatility can be annualized by scaling it by the square root of time (√12 for a year). This assumes returns are independent month-to-month. Annualized volatility is the standard way to compare risk across assets and time horizons in equity research.
computation: Calculate or obtain monthly standard deviation
Multiply by √12 (approximately 3.464)

worked_example.problem: Nifty 50 monthly standard deviation is 3.03%. Annualize it.
worked_example.insight: The monthly volatility of 3.03% compounds to an annualized volatility of 10.5%. This is the number used in CAPM, portfolio risk calculations, and earnings volatility models.
